must_remember: Newton's First Law defines inertial reference frames and introduces inertia and mass qualitatively.
Newton's Second Law establishes $F = \frac{dp}{dt} = ma$ for constant mass systems, adhering to the principle of independent orthogonal components.
Newton's Third Law states action and reaction forces act on different bodies and therefore do not cancel out.
Static friction $f_s \le \mu_s N$ self-adjusts up to a maximum limit, whereas kinetic friction $f_k = \mu_k N$ is constant during relative sliding.
Non-inertial frames require fictitious forces like centrifugal force $F_{cf} = -m \vec{\omega} \times (\vec{\omega} \times \vec{r})$ and Coriolis force $F_{cor} = -2m (\vec{\omega} \times \vec{v}')$.
The Tsiolkovsky rocket equation governs variable-mass systems: $v = v_0 + v_e \ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m}\right)$.

glossary.meaning: A reference frame in which Newton's law of inertia holds true, characterized by zero net force yielding zero acceleration.
An accelerated reference frame requiring the incorporation of fictitious forces to apply Newton's laws correctly.
The integral of force over time, equal to the change in linear momentum ($J = \int F dt = \Delta p$).
A contact force that opposes impending relative motion between two surfaces up to a maximum limit $f_{s,max} = \mu_s N$.
A fictitious deflective force experienced by moving objects within a rotating non-inertial reference frame.
